newsitem.title: cambodia: Cambodian royalists expel five senior officials.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian royalists expel five senior officials.

text.p: Cambodia's royalist FUNCINPEC party on Friday expelled five senior officials who had challenged the leadership of co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh and will seek to remove them from government and parliament.

A meeting of 30 members of the 35-strong party steering committee voted unanimously to expel dissident leader Ung Phan, influential provincial governors Toan Chhay and Duong Khem, deputy provincial governor Ka Lean and a deputy regional military commander, Chen Sambo, officials later told reporters.

A resolution, read to journalists and signed by FUNCINPEC leader Ranariddh, said the party would also seek to remove the men from public office and, in the case of Minister of State Ung Phan, from his seat in the national assembly, or parliament.
Ranariddh, who presided over the meeting but avoided speaking to reporters, had earlier in the day dismissed the challenge to his leadership.
"FUNCINPEC is still strong, FUNCINPEC doesn't go down, FUNCINPEC doesn't crack. I am not worried," he told reporters at a school opening.

"They (Ung Phan and his supporters) are expecting 23 members of FUNCINPEC to support him, but you can see many members of parliament are with me today. It is clear that Mr Ung Phan will get very, very low (support)...," he added.

Ung Phan, a former senior member of the rival Cambodian People's Party (CPP) led by co-Premier Hun Sen, issued a statement on April 15 saying he no longer recognised the prince's leadership and and blamed his policies for severe political tension between the two parties.
The CPP supported the statement of Ung Phan, adding to tension between the parties, which formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-run polls in 1993.
Pro-CPP media broadcast messages of support for Ung Phan from the other four men, who could not be reached for comment.

Ranariddh accused Hun Sen of interfering in the internal affairs of FUNCINPEC and the royalists believe Hun Sen is trying to engineer a split as part of a strategy that has divided other smaller parties in the past two years.

But while FUNCINPEC played down the importance of the break, some analysts believed the defections of stalwarts Toan Chhay and Duong Khem was a threat as they head two northwest provinces long seen as loyal to the royalists.

Deputy Premier Ing Kieth acknowledged they might have problems removing the men from their government posts as this would need the approval of Hun Sen, who has already stated that Ung Phan and others should retain their jobs.
Toan Chhay, whose defection came as the biggest surprise, has enjoyed the support of the military in his province of Siem Reap, but it was not known if FUNCINPEC officers would follow him.
Ranariddh stressed that his party had no plans to resort to violence and said that recent events did not, at least for the time being, signal the end of the coalition.

The Ung Phan case has brought tension between the FUNCINPEC and CPP to boiling point, following a deadly March 30 grenade attack against an demonstration led by opposition leader and FUNCINPEC ally, Sam Rainsy.

Tension has also been heightened by the unsuccessful attempt this week by former FUNCINPEC secretary-general Prince Norodom Sirivudh to return home from exile to fight his 1996 conviction on charges linked to an alleged plot to assassinate Hun Sen.
